allusions.nt_words: ἰδού ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρί ἕξει καί τέξεται υἱόν καί καλέσουσι(ν) τό ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουήλ
allusions.ot_mt_form: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ עִמָּנוּ אֵל (Behold, the young woman is pregnant and will bear a son, and she will call his name Immanuel)
allusions.ot_lxx_form: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Εμμανουηλ (Behold, the virgin will be with child and will bear a son, and you [singular] will call his name Emmanuel)
allusions.textual_implication: Matthew's use of παρθένος ('virgin') follows the LXX rendering rather than MT's עַלְמָה ('young woman'), a lexical choice with profound christological implications for the virginal conception. The verbal forms ἕξει καί τέξεται align closely with LXX syntax, though Matthew modifies the verb καλέσεις (2nd singular) to καλέσουσι(ν) (3rd plural), shifting agency from Isaiah's addressee to the broader community. This represents a careful adaptation of LXX Isaiah for Matthew's theological purposes while maintaining fidelity to the Greek textual tradition.
allusions.textual_implication_plain: Matthew quotes the Greek Old Testament (LXX) which uses 'virgin' instead of the Hebrew's 'young woman,' a difference crucial for Matthew's theology of Jesus's birth. He slightly modifies who does the naming to fit his narrative context.
allusions.scholarly_note: Beale & Carson note this as the paradigmatic case of LXX influence on NT christology, with the παρθένος rendering enabling Matthew's virgin birth narrative (pages 1-2).

summary_technical: Matthew 1:23 demonstrates clear dependence on LXX Isaiah 7:14, particularly in the crucial lexeme παρθένος, while introducing a minor grammatical modification (3rd plural verb) to accommodate narrative context. The citation exemplifies how NT authors worked from Greek OT texts and adapted them with theological precision.
summary_plain: Matthew quotes the Greek Old Testament version of Isaiah, which uses 'virgin' instead of 'young woman,' and makes a small change about who names the child.

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: LXX Vorlage Enables Matthean Virgin Birth Theology
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The textual form Matthew inherited (LXX's παρθένος) provided the lexical foundation for articulating virgin birth christology in a way the MT reading (עַלְמָה) would not have directly supported. Matthew's modification of the verbal form from singular to plural (καλέσουσι[ν]) demonstrates active engagement with the text rather than wooden reproduction, suggesting he viewed the LXX as authoritative scripture capable of contextual adaptation. This represents early Christian hermeneutical practice where textual form and theological interpretation were mutually reinforcing.
bibcrit_hypothesis.plain: The Greek Old Testament Matthew used already had the word 'virgin,' which gave him the biblical language he needed to explain Jesus's unique birth. He wasn't just copying but actively shaping the text to fit his Gospel story.

_validation.confidence_note: The core textual observations about παρθένος vs עַלְמָה and the verb form change are accurate and verifiable, but specific scholarly citation and one textual claim need qualification.

flagged_claims.claim: Beale & Carson note this as the paradigmatic case of LXX influence on NT christology, with the παρθένος rendering enabling Matthew's virgin birth narrative (pages 1-2)
flagged_claims.reason: The page reference '1-2' is suspicious and likely fabricated; the Matthew section in Beale & Carson's Commentary on the NT Use of the OT is authored by Craig Blomberg and discusses Matt 1:23 at specific pages, not 1-2. The phrasing 'paradigmatic case' is also not a verifiable direct attribution.

flagged_claims.claim: Matthew modifies the verb καλέσεις (2nd singular) to καλέσουσι(ν) (3rd plural)
flagged_claims.reason: LXX manuscripts of Isa 7:14 vary: some read καλέσεις (2nd sg), some καλέσει (3rd sg, closer to MT's וְקָרָאת read as 3fs), and some καλέσετε. Stating definitively that Matthew 'modified' the LXX assumes a specific Vorlage that may not match what Matthew used; he may have inherited a variant reading.

flagged_claims.claim: הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ
flagged_claims.reason: The MT actually reads וְקָרָאת as a form most often parsed as 2nd feminine singular ('and you shall call'), not 3rd person 'she will call' as the gloss states. This is a contested parsing but the translation given is not the standard reading.

safe_claims: Matthew's παρθένος matches LXX Isaiah 7:14 against MT's עַלְמָה
The verbal forms ἕξει καί τέξεται align with LXX Isaiah
The lexical choice παρθένος has christological significance for the virginal conception
Matthew 1:23 demonstrates dependence on Greek Isaiah rather than the Hebrew
